Context/Background: Perianal fistulizing Crohn’s disease (CD) is a severe gastrointestinal disorder causing extensive mucosal damage with limited treatment options. Severe manifestations of the disease appear at higher rates in non-Europeans but the genetic and cellular mechanisms driving the disease phenotypes remain poorly understood. Herein, we tested whether pathologic determinants in the epithelial stem cell compartment could be detected at the transcript level in rectal organoids derived from a diverse patient population. Rectal organoid and mucosal cells from endoscopic biopsies of each patient having perianal fistulizing CD or no disease controls were prepared for and sequenced at the single cell level. After cell type annotations based on expressed marker genes, samples were analyzed by principal components, for differential transcript expression, cell type proportions, and pathway enrichment.
Prompt: Pathway analysis of transcriptional data from the mucosal epithelial (undifferentiated) cells of different CD phenotypes was performed against the Reactome database.  CD phenotypes compared are PIF (Perianal CD inflamed) vs PNI (Perianal CD non inflamed), PIF vs Control (non IBD), and PIN vs Control.  Please give a summary of the pathway enrichment results.  Focus on comparisons involving the PIF (inflamed) group.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
Differential pathway enrichment (Reactome) was carried out on DE genes from undifferentiated mucosal epithelial cells comparing Perianal CD Inflamed (PIF) versus Non-inflamed (PNI) and versus non-IBD Controls.  Only down-regulated pathways achieved significance in both PIF contrasts; no up-regulated Reactome terms were reported.  For PIF versus Control, 105 genes in “Metabolism of RNA” were suppressed and for PIF versus PNI, 76 genes in the same pathway were suppressed.  All other enriched terms likewise reflect decreased activity in PIF epithelium.

Keywords  
• RNA metabolism  
• Translation  
• Mitochondrial energy metabolism  
• Cell cycle  
• Stress responses  

Candidate Genes  
FAU, LSM7, SNRPD1, MRPL41, NDUFB2, COX4I1, CDK4  

Pathway Enrichments  

PIF vs Control (all DOWN; top 6 by gene count)  
| Theme                                                              | Gene Count ↓ |  
|--------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------:|  
| Metabolism of RNA                                                  |         105  |  
| Translation                                                        |          77  |  
| The Citric Acid (TCA) Cycle and Respiratory Electron Transport     |          74  |  
| Cellular Responses to Stimuli                                      |          73  |  
| Cellular Responses to Stress                                       |          71  |  
| Respiratory Electron Transport & ATP Synthesis/Uncoupling Proteins |          66  |  

PIF vs PNI (all DOWN; top 6 by gene count)  
| Theme                                                      | Gene Count ↓ |  
|------------------------------------------------------------|-------------:|  
| Metabolism of RNA                                          |          76  |  
| Translation                                                |          67  |  
| The Citric Acid (TCA) Cycle and Respiratory Electron Transport |      61  |  
| Cell Cycle                                                 |          55  |  
| Cellular Responses to Stimuli                              |          55  |  
| Cellular Responses to Stress                               |          53  |  

Analysis  
1. In both PIF contrasts, 100% of significant Reactome pathways are down-regulated, indicating a pervasive repression of core epithelial functions in inflamed perianal CD.  
2. “Metabolism of RNA” and “Translation” show the largest gene-level suppression (105 vs Ctrl; 76 vs PNI), pointing to broad impairment of RNA processing and protein synthesis in PIF.  
3. Energy-production modules (TCA cycle, mitochondrial/respiratory electron transport) are among the most suppressed, suggesting mitochondrial dysfunction in inflamed epithelium.  
4. Cell cycle pathways are also significantly down, potentially reflecting reduced proliferation or stem cell activity under inflammation.  
5. Stress- and stimulus-response pathways (including TP53-mediated regulation and neutrophil degranulation) are repressed, implying altered epithelial defense and repair mechanisms in PIF.  

Targeted (keyword-guided) subset  
Filtering for “RNA,” “translation,” and “mitochondrial” recovers the top six pathways in both PIF contrasts, confirming that suppression of RNA metabolism, protein synthesis, and mitochondrial energy generation are the dominant PIF-associated signatures.  

Key Genes/Proteins (leading-edge)  

Upregulated in PIF: not observed  
Downregulated in PIF:  
| Gene   | Role/Function               | Pathway(s)                    |  
|--------|-----------------------------|-------------------------------|  
| FAU    | Ribosomal protein adapter   | Metabolism of RNA; Translation|  
| LSM7   | Pre-mRNA splicing           | Metabolism of RNA             |  
| SNRPD1 | snRNP core component        | Metabolism of RNA; Splicing   |  
| MRPL41 | Mitochondrial ribosomal L41 | Mitochondrial translation     |  
| NDUFB2 | ETC Complex I subunit       | Respiratory electron transport|  
| COX4I1 | ETC Complex IV subunit      | Respiratory electron transport|  
| CDK4   | G1/S cell cycle kinase      | Cell cycle                    |  

Implications  
The global down-regulation of RNA processing, translation, energy metabolism, and cell cycle in PIF mucosal epithelium suggests a shift toward impaired regenerative capacity and mitochondrial dysfunction under active inflammation.  Suppression of TP53-driven stress responses and neutrophil degranulation pathways may further compromise epithelial barrier repair and innate defense.  These insights highlight potential targets for restoring epithelial function (e.g., enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis or supporting RNA-processing machinery) in perianal fistulizing CD.

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Validate mitochondrial functional defects in PIF epithelium (e.g., Seahorse assays) and correlate with transcript suppression.  
2. Examine if boosting RNA-processing factors (e.g., overexpressing SNRPD1) rescues epithelial repair in organoids.  
3. Investigate whether CDK4 pathway agonists can restore proliferation deficits in PIF mucosal stem cells.  
4. Clarify whether similar pathway suppression occurs in differentiated epithelial cells or specific cellular subtypes (e.g., goblet vs enterocyte precursors).
